tldr: To tackle progressive robotic assembly, the authors propose PVRA, a framework that dynamically identifies the role of components from an RGB-D point cloud and simultaneously estimates both current grasp poses and post-assembly target poses via keypoint voting.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed PVRA framework. Back-projected point clouds from RGB-D images are processed to extract features, concurrently performing pointwise role segmentation (SEG), pre-assembly keypoint offset prediction (KpOF), and target offset prediction relative to the base component (AKpOF).
overview:
Assembling parts step by step is intuitive for humans, but remains exceptionally challenging for robots. Traditional robot vision has largely centered on "object-centric perception," focusing on locating objects in camera images and estimating their 6D poses (position and orientation). However, performing autonomous assembly requires "assembly context awareness"—understanding the temporal sequence of which part to move, geometric inter-part relationships regarding where to attach it, and stability under gravity.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed PVRA, a modular learning framework that takes a single RGB-D point cloud of an in-progress assembly scene. It dynamically identifies which part to move in the current step (the target part) and which part it attaches to (the base part), directly predicting the 6D poses of both at the same time. By having points in the point cloud cast votes (predict offsets) toward 3D keypoints of the objects, the system achieves pose estimation that is robust against noise and the partial occlusions common in ongoing assembly.

The authors validated their method on an assembly dataset for a planetary gearbox (Nema17), comparing it against a precise CAD registration baseline (CAD-ICP-PCA) and a state-of-the-art pose foundation model (FoundationPose). Without relying on ground-truth mask boundaries, PVRA reliably predicts target assembly poses directly from partial point clouds, demonstrating the value of assembly-specific vision that goes beyond object-centric perception.
contributions: Proposal of PVRA, a 3D keypoint-based integrated learning framework that provides context awareness (temporal, spatial, and inter-part relationships) for progressive robotic assembly
Formulation of an augmented set of evaluation metrics (such as SSA and SLA) to evaluate dynamic role segmentation (target, base, background) and 6D pose estimation across progressive assembly steps
Implementation and comprehensive benchmarking on a planetary gearbox (Nema17) assembly dataset against state-of-the-art object-centric baselines

sections.heading: Moving from Simple Object Recognition to Assembly Context Awareness
sections.summary: Standard object recognition and 6D pose estimation fall short when automating complex assembly operations. This chapter defines the concept of "assembly task awareness" (spatial, temporal, inter-part relationships, and physical stability) and motivates an end-to-end approach to learn it.
sections.details:
Putting components together into a finished product is vital across manufacturing, repair, surgical robotics, and space exploration. Yet, despite advances in deep learning and reinforcement learning, robots cannot yet truly understand and act upon the context of assembly tasks.

In robotic manipulation, 6 Degrees of Freedom (6 DoF) pose estimation—capturing the 3D position and orientation of an object—is standard. However, multi-part assembly demands far more than just recognizing what is there. It requires four key perception capabilities:

- Spatial awareness: Identifying the pre- and post-assembly poses of each component
- Temporal awareness: Understanding the optimal sequence for attaching components
- Relational awareness: Grasping inter-part relationships to maintain the structural integrity of the final product
- Physical stability awareness: Determining whether components will remain stable and resting under gravity

The authors collectively define these as "assembly task awareness." Moving beyond simple pick-and-place, this paper introduces PVRA (Pointwise Key-point Voting Framework for Robotic Assembly) as a module that interprets the current progress and directly infers actionable outputs.

sections.heading: From Geometric Planning to Learning-Based Assembly Pose Estimation
sections.summary: This section reviews related work in Assembly Sequence Planning (ASP) and Assembly Pose Estimation (APE). It traces the evolution from classical geometry-based combinatorial optimization to recent deep learning, transformers, and graph neural networks, setting the stage for occlusion-robust keypoint voting.
sections.details:
Assembly research originated in manufacturing engineering as Assembly Sequence Planning (ASP) and path planning.

### 2.1 Assembly Sequence Planning (ASP)
Methods seeking physically collision-free and feasible sequences include "Assemble them All," which uses physics-guided search, and "ASAP," which also factors in gravitational stability. These rely on the "Assembly by Disassembly" principle—assuming that reversing a valid disassembly path yields a viable assembly sequence. Recent approaches like "PAST" employ point cloud transformers to reason across multiple hierarchical levels.

### 2.2 Assembly Pose Estimation (APE)
APE focuses on estimating final target poses given a set of parts. While works like GPAT tackle mating unseen parts, many assume solving the entire assembly in a single step, ignoring intermediate states and ongoing physical constraints. In contrast, sequential inference models have emerged, including instance-encoding transformers and RGL-Net, which dynamically updates inter-part relationships using graph structures. Other methods explore neural shape mating via geometric symmetries or SE(3)-equivariant networks, but handling temporal dependencies and assembly ambiguities remains challenging.

### 2.3 Keypoint Methods and Assembly Datasets
Processing full point clouds directly is computationally heavy and noise-sensitive. Keypoint voting methods, such as PVNet and PVN3D, have proven robust to occlusion by having points vote for vectors pointing to representative keypoints. While PVRA draws inspiration from PVN3D's mechanism, it fundamentally repurposes it from single-object localization to assembly context awareness. Furthermore, because common datasets like PartNet lack sequential assembly progress, this work adopts the 6DApose dataset, which contains intermediate assembly steps and gravity-stable configurations.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Inferring the Moving Part and Target Pose from Point Clouds
sections.summary: The problem is framed as a supervised learning task: given an RGB-D image, identify the target component to manipulate at the current assembly step, its current grasp pose, and its target assembled pose relative to the base part.
sections.details:
Consider an assembly task comprising $C$ components. Rather than predicting all configurations at once, this study adopts a sequential approach that advances one part per step $t \in \{1, 2, \dots, C\}$.

To ensure practical evaluation and reproducibility, the paper establishes four working assumptions:

- The assembly sequence is predetermined and fixed
- For each step, the component to be assembled (target) and its target 6D pose are uniquely defined
- Each component rests in a physically stable pose under gravity
- The target component makes contact with exactly one mating component (base part) during assembly

Under this formulation, given an input RGB-D image $I_{RGB-D}$ in camera coordinates, the goal is to learn a mapping $f(I_{RGB-D})$ that identifies the target component $O_t$ at current step $t$, estimating its current pose $Q_t \in SE(3)$ and its target assembled pose $T_t \in SE(3)$ when attached to the base component.

sections.heading: PVRA Architecture: Unifying Role Segmentation and Keypoint Voting
sections.summary: The framework extracts fused features from RGB images and point clouds, jointly training three heads: pointwise role segmentation (SEG), target keypoint offset prediction (KpOF), and post-assembly keypoint offset prediction (AKpOF). Sparse 3D keypoints sampled from CAD models enable robust 6D pose recovery via offset voting.
sections.details:
PVRA accepts RGB-D inputs and directly predicts actionable outputs for robotic grasping and mating.

### 4.1 Feature Extraction and Dense Fusion
The depth image is back-projected into a 3D point cloud, sampling $N$ points containing 3D coordinates, RGB values, and surface normals. A pre-trained CNN (PSPNet with a ResNet-18 backbone) extracts semantic features from the RGB image, while PointNet++ extracts geometric features from the point cloud. These are concatenated per point (Dense Fusion) to form a shared feature map $F_t$.

### 4.2 Semantic Role Segmentation (SEG)
The SEG module predicts a probability distribution for each point $p$, classifying it into "target component," "base component," or "background." Crucially, unlike standard semantic segmentation, this captures dynamic roles: a component that acts as the target at step $t$ may become the base component in subsequent steps.

### 4.3 Keypoint Offset Prediction (KpOF / AKpOF)
Instead of directly regressing 6D poses, the model predicts offsets (Manhattan distances) to predefined 3D keypoints to derive poses.
- KpOF module: Predicts offsets $L_t$ from target points to pre-assembly keypoints of the target part, recovering the current grasp pose.
- AKpOF module: Predicts offsets $D_t$ from base points to the keypoints where the target part should reside after assembly, recovering the target assembly pose.

### 4.5 Keypoint Setup and Loss Functions
Keypoints are pre-defined by selecting 8 points per part from CAD models using Farthest Point Sampling (FPS). Choosing 8 points provides an effective spatial representation while keeping output dimensionality compact. During training, the SEG head uses Focal Loss, and the two offset heads use Smooth L1 Loss (Offset Loss). The network is trained end-to-end using a unified joint loss function.

captions.F1: Network architecture of PVRA. After fusing RGB features and depth point clouds, the network branches into three heads: SEG for pointwise role classification, KpOF for predicting the current target pose, and AKpOF for voting post-assembly target keypoints from base component points.

sections.heading: Quantitative Evaluation and Baseline Comparisons on a Planetary Gearbox
sections.summary: The method is evaluated on a sequential assembly dataset of a Nema17 gearbox (8,620 instances). Benchmarked against CAD registration (ICP) and a recent foundation model (FoundationPose), PVRA's performance is analyzed using assembly-specific metrics (SSA, SLA).
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
Evaluations were conducted on a simulated sequential assembly dataset of a Nema17 planetary gearbox (5 components, 4 steps, totaling 8,620 instances), partitioned into 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% testing. Training was performed using four NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs (32GB each).

Baselines included CAD-ICP-PCA (initial alignment via Principal Component Analysis followed by ICP refinement) and FoundationPose, a state-of-the-art CAD-based foundation model for pose estimation. Baselines were provided ground-truth component roles and relative transformation matrices in advance, whereas PVRA had to infer all of these autonomously from observed point clouds. Baselines were evaluated both with ideal ground-truth masks (GT-masks) and with noisy masks predicted by PVRA (PVRA-predicted-masks).

### 5.2 Evaluation Metrics
- SSA (Step-Segmentation Accuracy): Mean IoU of target and base role segmentation, assessing temporal and relational accuracy.
- SLA (Step-Localization Accuracy): Maximum Symmetry-aware Surface Distance (MSSD) normalized by component diameter $d$. The primary threshold used is $0.15d$ (Step Acc@0.15d), alongside Area Under the Curve (AUC) for holistic assessment.

### 5.3 Quantitative Results
At the $0.15d$ threshold, PVRA achieved a high success rate of 0.8929 (89.29%) in Step Acc@0.15d. As seen in Figure F2, PVRA's accuracy rises sharply between $0.05d$ and $0.15d$. While FoundationPose with ground-truth masks (FP-GT) achieves superior accuracy under strict tolerances, feeding it PVRA-predicted masks (FP-PVRA) leads to 53 failed inference cases due to missing boundaries, causing accuracy to plateau. Meanwhile, CAD-ICP-PCA struggled significantly throughout due to its sensitivity to partial occlusion.

captions.F2: Step accuracy curves against normalized MSSD thresholds. PVRA (solid blue line) closely follows FoundationPose with ground-truth masks (dashed green line), reaching nearly 90% accuracy around 0.15d.

sections.heading: Why Keypoint Voting Fits Progressive Assembly
sections.summary: This section unpacks key findings: the failure modes of ICP on partial point clouds, robustness against imperfect mask boundaries, the benefit of end-to-end relationship prediction without prior knowledge, and the transfer gap from simulation to reality.
sections.details:
The experimental results highlight several critical insights.

First, conventional CAD alignment via ICP is fragile when applied to partial point clouds and the severe occlusions typical of mating parts. Even with ground-truth segmentation masks, ICP struggled to achieve high accuracy.

Second, even powerful models like FoundationPose rely heavily on crisp, dense masks. When supplied with PVRA's predicted point masks, FoundationPose failed to output poses for 53 samples due to small part sizes and ambiguous boundaries. In contrast, PVRA's pointwise voting design allows remaining visible points to cast accurate keypoint votes, maintaining stable overall AUC scores even with imperfect masks.

Third, PVRA eliminates the need for prior knowledge. Baseline methods require external guidance specifying which component is the target, which is the base, and what transformation relates them. PVRA, however, infers what to move and where to place it directly from its learned internal representations using just a single RGB-D image.

The average diameter of Nema17 parts is roughly 51 mm, meaning the $0.15d$ evaluation threshold corresponds to an absolute surface distance error of about 7–8 mm. While physical insertion may ultimately require fine-grained force control or near-field visual servoing, this level of accuracy is well-suited for coarse approach and bringing parts to initial mating configurations (actionable outputs).

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work: From Assembly to General Task Awareness
sections.summary: This work proposed and validated PVRA, a keypoint-based framework that captures temporal, spatial, and inter-part relationships in progressive assembly. Looking ahead, this task-aware perception can extend beyond assembly to diverse contact-rich manipulation tasks.
sections.details:
This paper introduced PVRA, a keypoint-based modular learning framework that models task context for sequential robotic assembly. Compared to object-centric alternatives, it operates robustly under partial point clouds and occlusions, directly producing actionable outputs required for assembly.

Future work includes Sim-to-Real adaptation to handle sensor noise and lighting variations present in real environments, as well as extending the framework to flexible sequences without fixed assembly orders. Reasoning over operational phases and geometric dependencies represents an important step toward generalizing robot perception across broad manipulation tasks.

takeaways: Robotic assembly requires assembly task awareness—capturing dynamic roles, temporal sequences, and relative part layouts—rather than isolated single-object poses.
Pointwise keypoint voting (KpOF/AKpOF) enables robust pose estimation despite partial occlusions and incomplete segmentation boundaries common in progressive assemblies.
Directly predicting the target part's assembled pose as an offset from the observed point cloud of the mating base part is highly effective.
Achieving roughly 89.3% accuracy within a 7–8 mm (0.15d) error margin on 51 mm components provides an actionable guidance pose for initial manipulator approaches and mating phases.
limitations: Validation is currently confined to a synthetic dataset (Nema17 gearbox), leaving Sim-to-Real transfer under real sensor noise, calibration errors, and specular reflections unverified.
The approach relies on simplifying assumptions: a strictly fixed assembly sequence and contact with only a single base component at each step.
Eight 3D keypoints must be pre-sampled from CAD models using FPS, precluding zero-shot assembly on completely novel, unseen part geometries.
